title: DID GOD CREATE EVIL?
paragraphs:
DID GOD CREATE EVIL?
The Question That Has Haunted Humanity for Thousands of Years—And the Answer That Changes Everything
What if one question has been silently following you your entire life?
Maybe you never said it out loud.
Maybe it surfaced when you stood beside a grave.
Maybe it appeared after betrayal shattered your trust.
Maybe it came after a diagnosis, a tragedy, a war, an abuse, a disaster, or a night when your prayers seemed to hit the ceiling and fall back down unanswered.
It is one of the oldest questions in human history.
It is also one of the most dangerous.
Because hidden underneath that question is another one:
For many people, the answer to that question determines everything.
And perhaps even now, as you read this, part of you is wrestling with it.
Because evil is not merely a theological concept.
A night you wish never happened.
So before we answer the question, we must understand something crucial.
The Bible never asks us to pretend evil is small.
Scripture stares directly into humanity's darkest realities without flinching.
The Bible contains murder, betrayal, rape, genocide, greed, corruption, war, hatred, deception, and rebellion.
And that honesty is exactly why its answer matters.
The opening words of Scripture establish a foundation that cannot be ignored:
"In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." (Genesis 1:1)
Everything that exists ultimately traces back to God as Creator.
Yet after every stage of creation, God repeatedly declares something remarkable.
"And God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was very good."
Evil was not part of God's original creation.
So where did evil come from?
Evil is not a created thing.
Evil is a corruption of a good thing.
Just as darkness is not a substance but the absence of light.
Just as cold is the absence of heat.
Just as a hole in a garment is not created fabric but damaged fabric.
Evil is not something God manufactured.
Evil is what happens when created beings rebel against God's goodness.
The first rebellion appears among spiritual beings.
The prophet Isaiah speaks of a proud heavenly figure whose heart became corrupted.
"You said in your heart, 'I will ascend to heaven.'"
Ezekiel 28 similarly describes one who was originally blameless until wickedness was found in him.
In Genesis 3, evil enters human history through a choice.
God created Adam and Eve with genuine freedom because love without choice is not love at all.
A forced relationship is not a relationship.
For love to be real, choice must be real.
And where choice exists, rejection becomes possible.
And the consequences exploded through creation.
"Sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin."
It was not created by God and inserted into creation.
Some people immediately raise another question.
If God knew evil would happen, isn't He still responsible?
That question deserves an honest answer.
God's foreknowledge is not the same as causation.
Knowing something will happen does not mean causing it.
Imagine a parent who knows their child is about to make a terrible decision.
The parent's knowledge does not create the decision.
Scripture repeatedly holds human beings responsible for their choices.
"God cannot be tempted with evil, and He Himself tempts no one."
The Greek text uses the word:
God is never the source of moral evil.
In fact, 1 John 1:5 makes one of the strongest declarations in all Scripture:
"God is light, and in Him is no darkness at all."
"There is absolutely no darkness in Him."
So why does Isaiah 45:7 seem to say God creates evil?
At first glance, that sounds decisive.
While "ra" can sometimes refer to moral evil, it often means disaster, calamity, judgment, distress, or catastrophe depending on context.
The verse is describing God's sovereignty over judgment and historical events, not moral wickedness.
The point is that God controls history.
The verse is not teaching that God creates sin or wickedness.
The entire testimony of Scripture rejects that conclusion.
Yet there remains a deeper issue.
Perhaps the most important issue of all.
Even if God did not create evil, why does He allow it?
That question cannot be answered with clichés.
The Bible's answer ultimately leads us to a hill outside Jerusalem.
Because the greatest response God ever gave to evil was not an explanation.
When humanity unleashed its worst evil against the only truly innocent person who ever lived, something astonishing happened.
God transformed the greatest evil in history into the greatest good in history.
Acts 2:23 says Jesus was handed over and crucified by wicked men.
Yet through that evil came salvation for the world.
Only God can take what was intended for destruction and rewrite it into redemption.
Joseph understood this long before Calvary.
After being betrayed by his brothers, sold into slavery, falsely accused, imprisoned, and forgotten, he eventually stood before the very men who had ruined his life.
"You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good."
Joseph did not say the evil was good.
He said God brought good from it.
God does not call evil good.
God overrules evil with greater purposes.
This is the story of Scripture.
A shepherd boy becomes a king.
A prostitute becomes part of the Messiah's family line.
A thief dies beside Jesus and enters paradise.
A cross becomes an empty tomb.
Perhaps that is the deeper reason this question matters.
Because many people are not really asking whether God created evil.
They are secretly wondering whether the evil they have experienced—or committed—has permanently ruined their story.
They wonder if the addiction has gone too far.
If the betrayal cannot be repaired.
If the shame can never leave.
If the scars will always define them.
The Gospel answers with a thunderous no.
Jesus Christ stepped into humanity's darkness so darkness would not have the final word.
The cross proves that evil is powerful.
The empty tomb proves it is not ultimate.
The resurrection declares that God is still rewriting stories.
Maybe you clicked this article because of a theological question.
But perhaps God brought you here for a more personal reason.
Perhaps your real question is not:
"Can God redeem what evil has done to me?"
Because Christianity is not the story of people finding God.
It is the story of God pursuing broken people.
The Gospel is not about perfect people.

Jesus Christ entered a world scarred by evil, carried humanity's sin upon Himself, died in our place, rose from the dead, and now offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life to all who trust Him.
That is the center of the Christian faith.
And it is why the story does not end with evil.
And evil itself will finally be removed.
Until that day, we live in the tension between a fallen world and a coming kingdom.
But we do not live without hope.
Because Jesus has already entered the battlefield and secured the victory.
What part of your story are you still asking God to rewrite?
Someone reading your testimony may discover hope because of your honesty.
The enemy writes accusations, but Jesus writes redemption.
